opus-5.5.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun, it's great to be here.

I think autonomous driving will be the first large-scale deployment of what I call physical AI, AI that doesn't just live on a screen but moves through the real world. In the next five to ten years, I believe robotaxis and autonomous logistics will become commercially viable in many cities, starting in defined zones and gradually expanding. Within maybe fifteen or twenty years, I would expect the majority of new vehicles to have some form of high-level autonomy.

What that changes is not just how we get from A to B. Over a million people die in traffic accidents every year, and the vast majority of those are caused by human error. If autonomous systems are even several times safer than human drivers, and I believe eventually they can be ten times safer, that's an enormous humanitarian impact. Then there's time. People spend an hour or two a day commuting, and the car becomes a mobile living room, an office, a space to rest. Cities change too. If cars are shared and always moving, you need far less parking, and that land can become parks, housing, community space.

Household robots, I think, will come a bit later, because the home is actually a harder environment than the road. Roads have rules, lanes, traffic signals. A home is unstructured: every kitchen is different, objects are soft, fragile, cluttered, and you have children and pets. But with the progress in large models, multimodal perception, and what we call embodied intelligence, robots are learning to generalize much faster than before. In ten years I think we'll see useful robots doing specific tasks, cleaning, tidying, carrying things, assisting in elder care. In twenty to thirty years, a general-purpose home robot may be as common as a car or a washing machine today.

Elder care is especially important to me. China, Japan, Korea, and Europe are all aging very quickly, and we simply won't have enough caregivers. Robots that can help an elderly person get up, remind them to take medicine, detect a fall, or just keep them company could let people live independently and with dignity much longer.

Of course, none of this happens automatically. We have to get safety right, privacy right, and the question of responsibility right. A robot in your home sees everything, so trust is the foundation. That's why I keep saying we need to develop these technologies responsibly, with verifiable safety and clear boundaries, and have humans stay in control. If we do it well, I'm optimistic. Autonomous vehicles will give us back time and lives, and household robots will give us back care and companionship. That's a future worth building.

r001.rationale: The response predicts widespread vehicle autonomy but does not say human driving will feel as novel as seeing a horse-drawn carriage.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that humans may need special approval to drive.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that automated service will make human-operated service a premium experience.

r004.rationale: It predicts that a general-purpose home robot may be as common as a washing machine today, an equivalent commonplace household benchmark.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun. It's a pleasure to be here.

Let me start with a framing I've used for a long time. I think of the coming decades of AI in terms of three stages: information intelligence, physical intelligence, and biological intelligence. Information intelligence is what we've been living through with large language models, where AI understands and generates text, images, and code. Physical intelligence is when AI enters the physical world, and autonomous driving and robotics are the two most important carriers of that. Biological intelligence, further out, is when AI connects more directly with life itself, with brain-computer interfaces and so on. We are right now at the transition from the first stage into the second.

On autonomous driving specifically, I'm quite optimistic, and I'll say frankly that the trajectory has been more conservative than I predicted when I was still at Baidu. But the fundamentals haven't changed. Autonomous driving is, in a sense, the first large-scale robot. A car is a robot on wheels. Over the next ten years, I think robotaxis will go from operating in a handful of cities to being a normal part of urban mobility in many major cities in China and the United States. The technology question is largely answered. What remains is cost, regulation, and the pace of scaling. Within twenty to thirty years, I believe the majority of vehicle miles in cities will be driven by machines rather than humans.

What does that do to everyday life? Several things. First, safety. Over a million people die on roads globally each year, and the overwhelming majority of those deaths come from human error. If we can reduce that by even half, it's one of the largest public health achievements of this century. Second, time. The average commuter spends hundreds of hours a year behind a steering wheel. That time becomes available for work, rest, conversation. Third, the shape of cities. If cars are shared and autonomous, we need far fewer of them, and we need far less parking. Urban land that's currently devoted to storing idle vehicles can become housing, parks, and public space. So the change is not only about transportation. It's about how we design the places where we live.

Now, household robots are a different kind of challenge, and I want to be honest about the difficulty. Driving is a structured problem. The road has rules, lanes, and signs. A home has none of that. Every kitchen is different, every object is placed differently, and the tasks are long and require many steps of manipulation. For a long time the bottleneck was not the hardware but the brain. The robot didn't have the general understanding of the world to deal with that variability. That is precisely what has changed in the last few years. Large models give robots a foundation for understanding language, vision, and common sense that we simply didn't have before. So I think we are at a genuine inflection point.

In the first ten years, I expect household robots to be specialized. They'll do laundry folding, dish loading, basic cleaning, fetching things. They'll start in constrained settings like elderly care facilities and hospitals, where the need is acute and the economics work earlier. In twenty to thirty years, I think general-purpose robots in the home become common in the way that washing machines became common in the twentieth century. That's a transformation of domestic labor on the scale of the appliance revolution.

The social dimension matters enormously here, particularly for China. We have a rapidly aging population. By mid-century there will be hundreds of millions of people over sixty-five, and we will not have enough caregivers. Robots that can help an elderly person stand, bathe, take medication, and simply have someone to talk to are not a luxury. They're a necessity. I think this is where robotics will have its deepest human impact.

I'll close with two cautions. One is that we should not confuse demos with deployment. A robot doing a task once in a lab is very different from a robot doing it ten thousand times reliably in ten thousand different homes. The last ten percent of reliability takes the longest. The second is about trust and governance. When machines move in the physical world, mistakes have physical consequences. We need safety standards, clear accountability, and regulation that is neither too fast nor too slow. I've always believed that technology should be developed in a way that is safe, controllable, and beneficial, and that becomes most urgent precisely when AI steps out of the screen and into our homes and streets.

So, to summarize: in ten years, autonomous driving becomes mainstream in cities and robots start entering homes in limited roles. In thirty years, both are as ordinary as smartphones are today, and the way we live, work, and care for one another will have changed as a result.

r002.rationale: It mentions regulation and safety standards generally, but does not suggest humans will need special approval to drive.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that human-operated service may become a premium experience.

r004.rationale: It predicts general-purpose home robots will become common in twenty to thirty years, comparing their adoption to washing machines becoming common.

astra-6.text:
I think both will become part of everyday life, but the transition will be gradual. Over the next ten years, autonomous driving may become common in certain cities and on specific routes before it can handle every road and every condition. That could give people back time and make transportation more accessible, especially for older people and people who cannot drive. But safety has to be demonstrated, and regulation and infrastructure have to evolve alongside the technology.

In the home, the challenge is different. A robot has to deal with stairs, clutter, fragile objects, children—an environment that changes constantly. So I expect robots to start with specific tasks, such as cleaning, carrying things, or helping people with limited mobility. A reliable robot that does a few useful things well could already make a big difference.

Over twenty or thirty years, these systems could become much more capable. Imagine an older person living independently, with transportation available when needed and a robot helping with daily physical tasks. That is a very meaningful benefit. The question is not just how intelligent we can make these machines, but whether they are safe, affordable, and useful enough to improve people's lives.

sol-6.1.text:
I think both will gradually become part of everyday life, but the pace will be different. Autonomous driving operates in a more structured environment than a robot working inside a home. Even so, driving has to handle unusual situations safely, so progress will depend on reliability, cost, and public trust, as well as intelligence.

Over the next ten years, I would expect more autonomous services in defined areas—transportation, delivery, and logistics. Over twenty or thirty years, if these systems become sufficiently safe and affordable, they could change how we design cities and how people use their time. For older people and people who cannot drive, the biggest benefit could be greater independence.

Household robots are very exciting, but a home is a difficult environment. Every home is different, and even a simple task like clearing a table requires perception, planning, and careful physical interaction. I think we will first see robots doing a limited set of useful tasks, then gradually becoming more capable.

My hope is that these technologies will give people more time and help them live independently for longer. The important question is whether they can provide dependable help at a price ordinary families can afford.
